P3S2 · WALL-MODAL · Analysis Benchmarks

Membrane shear-wall cantilever — fundamental in-plane period vs exact Timoshenko beam

Membrane shear-wall cantilever — fundamental in-plane period converges to the exact Timoshenko beam

PASS −0.1913% error tolerance 0.5% 0.05047 s vs 0.050593 s
§2

Technical features tested

  • Production membrane wall shell (STRIX engine)
  • Self-weight mass through the production seismic-mass path
  • Exact Timoshenko cantilever frequency equation (no discretisation)
  • Shear coefficient κ = 10(1+ν)/(12+11ν) (Cowper)
  • Four-level mesh refinement 3×6 → 24×48
  • Reference independently checked by a converged 1-D Timoshenko FE
§3

Problem description

A shear wall is the stiffest lateral element of most buildings, and its in-plane period sets the spectral demand. This study checks that the production membrane wall of the STRIX engine reproduces the physics of a cantilever wall exactly as beam theory predicts. The wall is 3 m × 9 m, t = 200 mm, fixed at the base and braced out-of-plane at every node (the slab/diaphragm idealisation); its only mass is its self-weight, lumped by the production seismic-mass rule on the horizontal degrees of freedom. Because the vertical degrees of freedom carry no mass, the wall cross-section has no rotary inertia, so the matching beam theory is the Timoshenko cantilever without rotary inertia (bending and shear flexibility, translational inertia only). Its exact fundamental frequency is the first root of the characteristic determinant built from EIψ″ + κGA(w′ − ψ) = 0 and κGA(w″ − ψ′) + ρAω²w = 0 with w = ψ = 0 at the base and zero moment and shear at the top — Huang’s cantilever frequency equation with the rotary-inertia term removed. With Cowper’s κ = 0.845 (ν = 0.2) it gives T₁ = 0.0505932 s, about 6 % longer than the Euler-Bernoulli value — shear flexibility is not negligible at H/W = 3. The exact root was checked against a converged 1-D Timoshenko finite-element solution (agreement 7×10⁻⁷ %) and against the Euler limit when the shear stiffness is made rigid.

Reference solution

  1. Fundamental in-plane period — mesh 3×62π/ω₁, D(ω₁) = 0= 0.050593 s
  2. Fundamental in-plane period — mesh 6×122π/ω₁, D(ω₁) = 0= 0.050593 s
  3. Fundamental in-plane period — mesh 12×242π/ω₁, D(ω₁) = 0= 0.050593 s
  4. Fundamental in-plane period — mesh 24×482π/ω₁, D(ω₁) = 0= 0.050593 s

Exact Timoshenko cantilever without rotary inertia: characteristic determinant from EI ψ'' + κGA(w' − ψ) = 0, κGA(w'' − ψ') + ρAω²w = 0 with clamped–free boundary conditions (the frequency equation of T.C. Huang, J. Appl. Mech. 28 (1961) 579–584 with the rotary-inertia term removed); shear coefficient κ = 10(1+ν)/(12+11ν) (G.R. Cowper, J. Appl. Mech. 33 (1966) 335–340, rectangle). Independently checked against a converged 1-D Timoshenko finite-element solution (verification/internal/p3s2_timoshenko_selfcheck.ts).

Mesh convergence of T₁

MeshT₁ (s)Δ
3×60.05047 −0.2441%

24×480.050496 −0.1913%

The fundamental in-plane period approaches the exact value as the mesh is refined and settles about −0.19 % at 24×48. The remaining gap is a definition difference, not a discretisation error: the wall is a plane-stress continuum whose fixed base also restrains in-plane warping, while beam theory represents shear through the single coefficient κ; both effects are second order at H/W = 3. The tolerance (0.5 %) was fixed only after this study, not before it.

§8

Conclusion

PASS

The STRIX engine membrane wall reproduces the exact Timoshenko cantilever period at every mesh, converging to within two tenths of a percent of the exact value; the residual is the continuum-versus-beam definition gap. In-plane bending and shear stiffness of the production wall element, and the production self-weight mass path, are therefore consistent with classical beam theory. (The former edition of this card, which swept the artificial stabilisers of a third-party shell element, does not apply to the STRIX engine shell, which has no such parameters.)
